answer:
1. The animation shows how inflation wears down a fixed income check. It uses US consumer prices (CPI-U) as the example. Each bar is a possible starting month between 1947 and Aug 2006. The bar shows how much of the "first check" level a later check is worth, measured against that check's own starting level. The label marks it as illustrative.

2. Frame 1 shows only the chart, with a top line at 80.7%. Frame 2 adds a "typical level check" of 54.3%, "about half." Frames 4 to 6 add a row of 20 small blocks that fills in, and the text "level check there by about year 8." Frame 6 also adds a note that each check is compared with its own first check, in percentages and not dollars. The bars rise and fall depending on the starting month, with a deep trough around the mid-1960s to early 1970s.

3. A check that stays the same in dollars loses buying power as prices rise. In a typical case, it falls to about half its starting value, and it gets there around year 8 of a roughly 20-year window. The chart reads as a spread of historical outcomes. 80.7% is the top of that range, 54.3% is the typical case, and some starting months did much worse. The note says this is US history and not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no direct instruction. A viewer could take away that a flat payout loses a lot of buying power over time, so it's worth comparing a fixed payout against one that adjusts for inflation. I'd weigh that against the lower starting payment an adjusting option usually has. The animation doesn't make that comparison, and it doesn't address my two quote options.

5. The animation didn't say that. It only shows the erosion and says it isn't a forecast. The advice is my own conclusion, and it comes from my situation as a 64-year-old comparing two payout options.
